questions.sec: Pelvic brim, false/true pelvis & inlet diameters
questions.q: The pelvic brim is formed by all EXCEPT:
opts: Sacral promontory and sacro-iliac joint margin of ala
Upper border of ascending rami of pubic bone and pubic crest
questions.exp: The brim comprises promontory, ala margin, iliopectineal line, ascending rami and pubic crest – not the ischial tuberosities. (Book p483)

questions.sec: Pelvic brim, false/true pelvis & inlet diameters
questions.q: The part of the pelvis ABOVE the brim is the ______ and its role in labour is ______.
opts: False pelvis; no role in labour – it supports the uterus
True pelvis; the whole of labour
questions.exp: The false pelvis above the brim has no role in labour and supports the uterus. (Book p483)

questions.sec: Pelvic brim, false/true pelvis & inlet diameters
questions.q: The four parts of the TRUE pelvis are:
questions.exp: True pelvis = inlet, cavity, mid-pelvis and outlet. (Book p483)

questions.sec: Pelvic brim, false/true pelvis & inlet diameters
questions.q: The pelvic inlet lies at the level of the pelvic brim. Match the anteroposterior diameters: true conjugate, obstetric conjugate, diagonal conjugate.
opts: True conjugate 11 cm; obstetric conjugate 10.5 cm; diagonal conjugate 12 cm
True conjugate 10.5 cm; obstetric conjugate 11 cm; diagonal conjugate 13 cm
True conjugate 12 cm; obstetric conjugate 11 cm; diagonal conjugate 10.5 cm
All three diameters measure 11 cm in a normal gynaecoid pelvis
questions.exp: Anteroposterior diameters of the pelvic inlet: true conjugate (sacral promontory to upper border of pubic symphysis) 11 cm; obstetric conjugate (to the middle border) 10.5 cm, the smallest and most important; diagonal conjugate (to the lower border) 12 cm. (Book p483)

questions.sec: Pelvic brim, false/true pelvis & inlet diameters
questions.q: Which conjugate is described as the SMALLEST and most important?
questions.exp: The obstetric conjugate (10.5 cm) is smallest and most important. (Book p483)

questions.sec: Pelvic brim, false/true pelvis & inlet diameters
questions.q: The critical obstetric conjugate is the minimum diameter below which vaginal delivery is impossible; its value and the contracted-pelvis cut-off are:
opts: 10 cm; below 10 cm means contracted pelvis
11 cm; below 11 cm means contracted pelvis
12 cm; below 12 cm means contracted pelvis
9 cm; below 9 cm means contracted pelvis
questions.exp: The critical obstetric conjugate is 10 cm, and below it the pelvis is contracted and vaginal delivery impossible. (Book p483)

questions.sec: Pelvic brim, false/true pelvis & inlet diameters
questions.q: The transverse diameter of the inlet is measured between the two farthest points on the iliopectineal line and equals:
opts: 13 cm, which is greater than any antero-posterior diameter of the inlet
11 cm, which is the same as the true conjugate of the pelvic inlet
12 cm, which is the oblique diameter measured from the sacro-iliac joint
10 cm, which is the transverse diameter of the plane of least dimension
questions.exp: The transverse diameter of the inlet is about 13 cm; the true conjugate is 11 cm and the oblique diameter about 12 cm. (Book p483)

questions.sec: Pelvic brim, false/true pelvis & inlet diameters
questions.q: The oblique diameters of the inlet (12 cm) run from:
opts: From the sacro-iliac joint on one side to the iliopectineal eminence on the other
From one ischial spine straight across to the ischial spine opposite
From the symphysis pubis directly backwards to the sacral promontory
From one ischial tuberosity across to the opposite tuberosity
questions.exp: The oblique diameters run from a sacro-iliac joint to the opposite iliopectineal eminence and measure about 12 cm. (Book p483)

questions.sec: Pelvic brim, false/true pelvis & inlet diameters
questions.q: Fill up: The true conjugate of the pelvic inlet runs from the sacral promontory to the ______ and measures about ______ cm.
opts: upper margin of the symphysis pubis; 11
lower margin of the symphysis pubis; 13
questions.exp: The true conjugate is the shortest antero-posterior diameter of the inlet and cannot be measured clinically, so the diagonal conjugate is used instead. (Book p483)

questions.sec: Pelvic cavity: planes of greatest & least dimensions
questions.q: Contracted pelvis on clinical pelvimetry is flagged when:
opts: An obstetric conjugate below 10 cm, or a diagonal conjugate below 11.5 cm
A true conjugate below 12 cm, which is the usual threshold applied
A bituberous diameter below 10 cm measured at the pelvic outlet
An interspinous diameter below 10 cm in the mid-cavity
questions.exp: Clinical pelvimetry flags contraction when the obstetric conjugate is under 10 cm or the diagonal conjugate under 11.5 cm. (Book p484)

questions.sec: Pelvic cavity: planes of greatest & least dimensions
questions.q: The pelvic cavity lies at the level of the ischial spines between inlet and anatomical outlet. Its shape and walls are:
opts: A truncated cylinder, with a shallow anterior wall and a deep concave posterior wall
A true cylinder, with anterior and posterior walls of equal depth
Funnel shaped, with a deep anterior wall behind the pubic bone
Cuboid, with a flat posterior wall formed by the sacrum
questions.exp: The cavity is a truncated cylinder: the pubic bone is short in front, while the sacrum forms a long concave curve behind. (Book p484)

questions.sec: Pelvic cavity: planes of greatest & least dimensions
questions.q: Posterior boundary of the plane of GREATEST pelvic dimensions vs the plane of LEAST pelvic dimensions:
opts: Junction of S2–S3 vertebrae; junction of S4–S5 vertebrae
Junction of S4–S5; junction of S2–S3
questions.exp: Greatest plane posteriorly at S2–S3; least plane at S4–S5. (Book p484)

questions.sec: Pelvic cavity: planes of greatest & least dimensions
questions.q: Lateral extent of the plane of greatest dimensions and of the plane of least dimensions:
questions.exp: Greatest plane laterally at the obturator foramen; least plane at the ischial spines. (Book p484)

questions.sec: Pelvic cavity: planes of greatest & least dimensions
questions.q: AP and transverse diameters: plane of greatest dimensions vs plane of least dimensions.
opts: 12.5–13 cm and 13 cm; 11.5 cm and 10 cm (interischial/bispinous)
10 cm and 11 cm; 13 cm and 12 cm
13 cm and 12.5 cm; 10 cm and 11.5 cm
11.5 cm and 10 cm; 12.5–13 cm and 13 cm
questions.exp: Greatest plane AP 12.5–13 cm, transverse 13 cm; least plane AP 11.5 cm, transverse 10 cm bispinous. (Book p484)

questions.sec: Pelvic cavity: planes of greatest & least dimensions
questions.q: The bispinous (interischial) diameter of the plane of least dimensions is:
opts: The smallest pelvic diameter and the most important obstetrically
questions.exp: At 10 cm it is the smallest pelvic diameter and most important obstetrically. (Book p484)

questions.q: Match the pelvic plane with its description — 1) Plane of the inlet 2) Plane of greatest pelvic dimension 3) Plane of least pelvic dimension … A) Lies at the level of the ischial spines, with an antero-posterior diameter of about 11.5 cm B) A rounded inlet with a transverse diameter of about 13 cm C) The roomiest plane, with an antero-posterior diameter of about 12.75 cm
questions.exp: The inlet is widest transversely, the mid-plane at the spines is the narrowest, and the plane of greatest dimension lies between them. (Book p484)

questions.q: The mid-pelvis is said to be CONTRACTED when the interischial diameter is:
questions.exp: Interischial diameter <8 cm defines mid-pelvic contraction. (Book p485)

questions.q: The clinical bedside clue to a contracted mid-pelvis is:
opts: Both ischial spines can be touched at once with the fingers of one hand
Neither ischial spine can be reached at all on vaginal examination
The sacral promontory is easily reached and projects prominently forward
The subpubic arch is unusually wide and the side walls are divergent
questions.exp: The bedside clue to a contracted mid-pelvis is being able to touch both ischial spines simultaneously with the fingers of the same hand. (Book p485)

questions.q: The pelvic outlet (anatomical) lies at the level of the:
questions.exp: The anatomical outlet is at the ischial tuberosities. (Book p485)

questions.q: Boundaries and diameters of the pelvic outlet:
opts: Tip of the coccyx, ischial tuberosities; AP 13 cm; transverse bituberous 11 cm
Sacral promontory, ischial spines; AP 11 cm; transverse 13 cm
Tip of the coccyx, ischial spines; AP 10 cm; transverse 10 cm
Ischial spines, ischial tuberosities; AP 12 cm; transverse 12 cm
questions.exp: The pelvic outlet is bounded posteriorly by the tip of the coccyx and laterally by the ischial tuberosities; its AP diameter is 13 cm and its transverse (bituberous) diameter is 11 cm. (Book p485)

questions.q: In relation to the outlet, the plane of least pelvic dimensions lies ______ and the plane of pelvic outlet ______.
questions.exp: The least-dimensions plane is superior and the outlet plane inferior. (Book p485)

questions.q: The posterior sagittal diameter of the MID-PELVIS is measured from the sacrum to the:
questions.exp: Mid-pelvic posterior sagittal diameter runs sacrum-to-spine and should be ≥5 cm. (Book p486)

questions.q: The posterior sagittal diameter of the OUTLET extends between:
opts: The ischial tuberosities and the tip of the coccyx
questions.exp: Outlet posterior sagittal diameter joins tuberosity and coccyx tip. (Book p486)

questions.q: The angle of inclination of the pelvis is the angle the pelvic inlet makes with the horizontal, equal to:
questions.exp: The inclination angle is 55°. (Book p486)

questions.q: The sub-pubic angle is the angle between the descending rami of the pubic bones; in males it is ______ and in females ______.
questions.exp: Males have an acute and females an obtuse sub-pubic angle. (Book p486)

questions.q: Fill up: The pelvic outlet has an antero-posterior diameter of about ______ cm and an intertuberous transverse diameter of about ______ cm.
questions.exp: The outlet AP diameter runs from the lower border of the symphysis to the tip of the sacrum and the bituberous diameter between the ischial tuberosities. (Book p486)

questions.sec: Significance of the ischial spine & stations
questions.q: Station of the fetal head is defined with respect to the:
questions.exp: Stations are referenced to the ischial spines. (Book p487)

questions.sec: Significance of the ischial spine & stations
questions.q: On the station scale from inlet to outlet, the inlet and outlet correspond to:
opts: -5 at the inlet, +5 at the outlet, and 0 at the ischial spines
0 at the inlet, +5 at the outlet, and -5 at the ischial spines
-3 at the inlet and +3 at the outlet, 0 at the ischial spines
-5 at the inlet and 0 at the outlet, -3 at the ischial spines
questions.exp: On the station scale from inlet to outlet, the inlet is -5, the outlet is +5, and 0 is at the ischial spines. (Book p487)

questions.sec: Significance of the ischial spine & stations
questions.q: The fetal head is considered ENGAGED at which station?
questions.exp: Engagement equals 0 station at the ischial spines. (Book p487)

questions.sec: Significance of the ischial spine & stations
questions.q: Forceps or vacuum application requires a station of at least:
questions.exp: Instrumental delivery needs station ≥ +2. (Book p487)

questions.sec: Significance of the ischial spine & stations
questions.q: Internal rotation of the fetal head and deep transverse arrest both occur at the level of the:
questions.exp: Both internal rotation and deep transverse arrest relate to the ischial spine level. (Book p487)

questions.sec: Significance of the ischial spine & stations
questions.q: Which muscle hangs from the ischial spine 'like a hammock'?
questions.exp: Levator ani suspends from the ischial spine. (Book p487)

questions.sec: Significance of the ischial spine & stations
questions.q: The ischial spine is the landmark for pudendal nerve block; access requires piercing the ______ and the indication is ______.
questions.exp: The sacrospinous ligament is pierced for pudendal block, used for instrumental delivery. (Book p487)

questions.sec: Significance of the ischial spine & stations
questions.q: All of the following statements about the ischial spines are true EXCEPT:
opts: They are the landmark for the plane of the pelvic inlet
They mark the plane of least pelvic dimension
They are the reference point used to define fetal head station
They can be felt on vaginal examination lateral to the mid-line of the pelvis
questions.exp: The ischial spines define the mid-pelvis and station zero, not the inlet, which is bounded by the sacral promontory and symphysis pubis. (Book p487)

questions.q: Match contracted pelvis cut-offs: inlet, mid-pelvis, outlet.
opts: OC < 10 cm / DC < 11.5 cm; interischial < 8 cm; bituberous < 8 cm
OC < 11 cm; interischial < 10 cm; bituberous < 10 cm
DC < 10 cm; interischial < 9 cm; bituberous < 9 cm
OC < 9 cm; interischial < 7 cm; bituberous < 7 cm
questions.exp: Inlet OC <10/DC <11.5 cm; mid-pelvis interischial <8 cm; outlet bituberous <8 cm. (Book p488)

questions.q: The BEST method of diagnosing a contracted pelvis and the stance on routine pelvimetry:
opts: Clinical pelvimetry; routine pelvimetry is not recommended
X-ray pelvimetry, which should be done routinely
Magnetic resonance imaging pelvimetry done routinely
External pelvimetry alone, with no internal assessment
questions.exp: The best method of diagnosing a contracted pelvis is clinical pelvimetry; routine pelvimetry is not recommended. (Book p488)

questions.q: Management of a contracted pelvis and its implication for future deliveries:
opts: Caesarean section, since vaginal delivery is contraindicated, and it commits her to repeat sections
A trial of labour is always attempted first, whatever the degree of contraction
Instrumental delivery once the cervix has reached full dilatation
Induction of labour with oxytocin from 38 completed weeks onwards
questions.exp: A genuinely contracted pelvis precludes vaginal delivery, and the indication recurs in every subsequent pregnancy. (Book p488)

questions.q: Pelvic variations: Naegele's pelvis and Robert's pelvis differ by:
opts: Naegele's – one ala of sacrum absent; Robert's – both alae absent
Naegele's – both alae absent; Robert's – one ala
Naegele's – flat pelvis; Robert's – funnel pelvis
questions.exp: Naegele's lacks one sacral ala; Robert's lacks both. (Book p488)

questions.q: Cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD) means:
opts: Either a fetus too large or a pelvis too small for each other, in a pelvis that may itself be normal
A maternal pelvis that is always contracted, whatever the size or position of the fetus
A fetus that is always macrosomic, whatever the size of the maternal pelvis
An absolute bony abnormality of the maternal pelvis in every single case
questions.exp: CPD is a relative mismatch between passenger and passage, so it can occur with a normal pelvis and a normal-sized baby. (Book p488)

questions.q: CPD can be located at which levels?
questions.exp: CPD may affect inlet, cavity or outlet. (Book p488)

questions.q: Rank the diagnostic methods for CPD:
opts: Trial of labour (best) > MRI > clinical pelvimetry
Clinical pelvimetry > MRI > trial of labour
questions.exp: Trial of labour is best, then MRI, then clinical pelvimetry. (Book p488)

questions.q: Indicators of CPD during labour include:
opts: Slow progress, marked caput and moulding, arrest of labour and the signs of obstructed labour
Rapid progress with early engagement of the head in the pelvic cavity
Complete absence of moulding, with a head that stays freely ballottable above the brim
Early spontaneous delivery with no caput and a short, easy second stage
questions.exp: Caput, moulding, slow progress and eventually obstructed labour with Bandl's ring are the clinical markers of disproportion. (Book p488)

questions.q: Management of CPD at the INLET by severity:
opts: Moderate or severe: caesarean; mild: a trial of labour
All degrees: caesarean section without a trial
All degrees: a trial of labour aiming for vaginal delivery
Mild: caesarean section; severe: a trial of labour
questions.exp: For CPD at the inlet, moderate or severe disproportion needs caesarean section, while mild disproportion allows a trial of labour. (Book p488)

questions.q: CPD at the OUTLET is managed by:
questions.exp: Outlet CPD mandates C-section. (Book p488)

questions.q: A primigravida at term is fully dilated but the head shows no descent after two hours of good contractions, with increasing caput and moulding and three-fifths of the head still palpable abdominally. What is the diagnosis and management?
opts: Cephalopelvic disproportion — deliver by caesarean section
Normal progress — allow another two hours of pushing
Uterine inertia — start high-dose oxytocin augmentation
Deep transverse arrest — attempt manual rotation and forceps delivery
questions.exp: Failure of descent after two hours of adequate contractions with caput and moulding means disproportion, not inertia, so oxytocin would be dangerous. (Book p488)

questions.q: What is the role of instrumental delivery in CPD?
questions.exp: Instrumental delivery has no role in CPD. (Book p489)

questions.q: True or false: CPD in the current pregnancy is an indication for recurrent C-section in the next pregnancy.
opts: False – CPD applies to the current fetus only, so it is not an indication
True – a repeat caesarean section should always be performed next time
True – but only when the disproportion was severe in this labour
False – but it means induction of labour is needed next time
questions.exp: False: CPD is relative to the current fetus only and is not an indication for recurrent caesarean section. (Book p489)

questions.q: CPD in the current pregnancy, irrespective of extent, is a contraindication for:
questions.exp: Any CPD contraindicates VBAC. (Book p489)

questions.q: The Caldwell-Moloy classification names four pelvic types; the m/c and least common are:
questions.exp: Gynaecoid is commonest; platypelloid rarest. (Book p489)

questions.q: Match pelvic type to representative shape: gynaecoid, android, anthropoid, platypelloid.
questions.exp: Gynaecoid = female, android = male, anthropoid = ape-like, platypelloid = bowl-shaped. (Book p489)

questions.q: Shape of the inlet in each type:
opts: Gynaecoid transverse oval; android heart shaped; anthropoid vertical/AP oval; platypelloid flat bowl
Gynaecoid heart shaped; android transverse oval; anthropoid flat; platypelloid AP oval
questions.exp: Inlet shapes follow the table: transverse oval, heart shaped, vertical/AP oval and flat bowl. (Book p489)

questions.q: Transverse vs AP diameters: which types show TD > AP, AP > TD and TD >> AP?
opts: Gynaecoid and android TD > AP; anthropoid AP > TD; platypelloid TD >> AP
Gynaecoid AP > TD; android TD >> AP
Anthropoid TD > AP; platypelloid AP > TD
questions.exp: TD > AP in gynaecoid/android, AP > TD in anthropoid, TD >> AP in platypelloid. (Book p489)

questions.q: Side walls of the pelvis by type:
opts: Gynaecoid parallel & broad; android convergent; anthropoid parallel & narrow; platypelloid divergent
Gynaecoid convergent; android divergent; anthropoid broad; platypelloid narrow
questions.exp: Wall configuration distinguishes the four types as listed. (Book p489)

questions.q: Prominent ischial spines and an acute sub-pubic angle characterise which pelvic type?
questions.exp: Android pelvis shows prominent spines (+) and an acute sub-pubic angle; gynaecoid has an obtuse angle and non-prominent spines. (Book p489)

questions.q: The sub-pubic angle in the gynaecoid pelvis is:
questions.exp: Gynaecoid pelvis has an obtuse sub-pubic angle. (Book p489)

questions.q: Match the Caldwell-Moloy pelvic type with its features — 1) Gynaecoid 2) Android 3) Anthropoid … A) A rounded or slightly oval inlet with a well-curved sacrum and roomy fore-pelvis, the favourable female pelvis B) A wedge-shaped inlet with convergent side walls, a narrow fore-pelvis and a shallow sacro-sciatic notch C) A long oval inlet with a generous antero-posterior diameter, favouring occipito-posterior positions
questions.exp: Gynaecoid is favourable, android predisposes to deep transverse arrest, and anthropoid favours direct occipito-posterior delivery. (Book p489)

units.title: Pelvic brim, false/true pelvis & inlet diameters
units.guide: Build the pelvic brim from its five landmarks, separate false from true pelvis and memorise the inlet conjugates, transverse and oblique diameters. Focus for this checkpoint: Pelvic brim, false/true pelvis & inlet diameters.

units.title: planes of greatest & least dimensions
units.guide: Compare the plane of greatest with the plane of least pelvic dimensions and learn why the 10 cm bispinous diameter dominates obstetrics. Focus for this checkpoint: Pelvic cavity: planes of greatest & least dimensions.

units.title: Mid-pelvis & pelvic outlet → Sagittal diameters & pelvic angles
units.guide: Detect mid-pelvic and outlet contraction by their diameters, then add the posterior sagittal diameters, inclination angle and sub-pubic angle. Focus for this checkpoint: Mid-pelvis & pelvic outlet, Sagittal diameters & pelvic angles.

units.title: Significance of the ischial spine & stations
units.guide: Use the ischial spine for stations, engagement, internal rotation, deep transverse arrest, levator ani attachment and the pudendal block landmark. Focus for this checkpoint: Significance of the ischial spine & stations.

units.title: Contracted pelvis & cephalopelvic disproportion
units.guide: Apply contraction cut-offs at inlet, mid-pelvis and outlet, then diagnose and manage CPD by level and severity with trial of labour as the best test. Focus for this checkpoint: Contracted pelvis & cephalopelvic disproportion.

units.title: CPD notes & Caldwell-Moloy pelvic types
units.guide: Remember that CPD is fetus-relative and bars VBAC, then classify gynaecoid, android, anthropoid and platypelloid pelves by inlet shape, walls and angles. Focus for this checkpoint: CPD notes & Caldwell-Moloy pelvic types.
